evidenceAudit.scope: Febrile seizures in children aged 6–60 months in India: definitions, excluding meningitis, investigations, treatment of a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, admission, intermittent and continuous prophylaxis, antipyretics and parent counselling, built on the IAP Tamil Nadu State Chapter COPP module on febrile seizures (2017).
findings: Definitions (simple, complex, febrile status above 30 minutes), recurrence risk factors, lumbar puncture indications (under 6 months; 6–12 months if Hib or pneumococcal vaccination incomplete; meningitis signs; prior antibiotics), limited role of EEG and imaging, acute benzodiazepine doses (diazepam 0.3–0.5 mg/kg IV, lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, midazolam 0.2 mg/kg, rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg), admission criteria, no benefit of antipyretics on recurrence, intermittent clobazam 0.3 mg/kg 12-hourly or diazepam 0.33 mg/kg 8-hourly for 24 hours from fever onset, continuous valproate 20–30 mg/kg/day or phenobarbitone 3–5 mg/kg/day for 2 years or to age 6, checked against the IAP COPP module (2017).
Paracetamol 15 mg/kg (oral loading 20 mg/kg), maximum 90 mg/kg/day oral and 60 mg/kg/day IV (10–50 kg), checked against the Gloucestershire children's analgesia guideline (2020).
unverifiedSections: The source is a state-chapter IAP teaching module, not a national IAP guideline.
Paracetamol for comfort is dosed from the Gloucestershire children's analgesia guideline because the IAP module gives no dose.

Buccal or intranasal midazolam dose and maximum benzodiazepine doses are taken from the IAP Standard Treatment Guidelines on status epilepticus (2022), because the COPP module names these routes without a dose.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Febrile seizures are the commonest seizures in childhood, affecting children aged 6 months to 5 years with fever but no brain infection or metabolic cause. Most are simple — generalised, under 15 minutes and not repeated within 24 hours — and carry an excellent prognosis with only about 1% later epilepsy risk. The key clinical task is to exclude meningitis, especially in infants and under-immunised children. Seizures over 5 minutes are treated with a benzodiazepine. Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence. Intermittent clobazam during fevers is reserved for frequent or complex seizures, and continuous drugs are rarely needed. Calm, clear counselling of parents is central. Recurrence occurs in about 30%, and is most likely when the first seizure happens before 1 year of age, with a short fever-to-seizure interval, at a low temperature, or with a family history.
keyMechanisms: The immature brain has a lower seizure threshold with rapid temperature rise.
Genetic predisposition: family history is a major risk factor.
Viral infections (including roseola and influenza) are common triggers.
Febrile seizures mark predisposition rather than cause epilepsy.

symptoms: Fever with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure
Fever for less than 24 hours before the seizure (a major recurrence risk factor) (IAP)
Brief post-ictal sleepiness with return to normal within an hour
physicalSigns: Temperature at presentation (a lower temperature at seizure onset predicts recurrence) (IAP)
redFlags: Meningeal signs, persistent drowsiness, petechial rash
Seizure over 5 minutes: treat as status (IAP)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, persistent drowsiness or prolonged post-ictal state; lumbar puncture and CSF analysis settle it (IAP).
Shivering and chattering with preserved consciousness and no post-ictal phase; observation of the episode settles it.
Pallor and limpness with brief jerks after standing or a vasovagal trigger, rapid recovery; history and normal examination settle it.
Previous afebrile seizures, focal features or developmental delay; EEG and neurology review settle it (IAP).
Diarrhoea, vomiting or poor intake with abnormal sodium, calcium or glucose; blood tests settle it (IAP).

differentials.condition: Dravet syndrome or other genetic epilepsy
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Prolonged, focal or very frequent febrile seizures starting before 1 year; neurology review and genetic testing settle it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Seizure with fever, age 6–60 months, no intracranial infection, metabolic cause or prior afebrile seizure.
Generalised, under 15 minutes, no recurrence in 24 hours.
Focal, 15–30 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours.

ruleIn.normalValue: Focus such as otitis; no meningism

clinicalManagement.title: During the seizure
actions: Protect the airway; turn the child on the side with head extended; prevent injury (IAP).
Time the seizure; secure IV access and check glucose if it continues (IAP).

clinicalManagement.title: Seizure over 5 minutes
actions: IV midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 5 mg), diazepam 0.3–0.5 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg) or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg); without IV access, rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg or buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.1–0.2 mg/kg (IAP; IAP STG 2022).
Still seizing 5–10 minutes after the first dose: repeat once, then second-line drugs on the status epilepticus pathway (IAP STG 2022; see Status epilepticus in children).

clinicalManagement.title: Admit or discharge
actions: Admit complex seizures and any child with signs of CNS infection or needing a lumbar puncture (IAP).
First simple seizure over 18 months, stable, parents educated: home; IAP lists lack of reliable family support as a possible reason to admit (IAP).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the fever source
actions: Find and treat the cause of fever (otitis, pneumonia, urinary infection, viral illness).
Paracetamol for comfort at 15 mg/kg; it does not prevent recurrence (IAP; Gloucestershire guideline).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevention
actions: Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence; use for comfort (IAP).
Intermittent clobazam (or oral or rectal diazepam) for frequent seizures, a previous complex seizure, poor access to care or seizures with risk factors (IAP).

clinicalManagement.title: Counsel parents
actions: Explain the benign nature, the about 30% recurrence risk and the low epilepsy risk (IAP).
Teach first aid and when to give rescue medicine or seek care; explain that fever medicine is for comfort only (IAP).

vignette.text: Ananya, a 20-month-old girl from Lucknow, is brought to the emergency department after a 3-minute generalised jerking episode at home with a temperature of 39.4°C. She had a runny nose and cough for a day. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, and 40 minutes later she is playing. She has completed all scheduled vaccines. Her father had febrile seizures as a child. Her mother asks whether this is epilepsy and whether to give fever medicine every few hours to stop another one.

guidedApproach.title: Why young children have febrile seizures
guidedApproach.prompt: What makes a 6–60 month old prone to seizures with fever?
guidedApproach.guidance: The developing brain has a lower seizure threshold, and a rapid rise in temperature during a viral illness can trigger a generalised seizure in a child who is genetically predisposed — a family history in a first-degree relative is one of the strongest risk factors. Febrile seizures are a marker of this age-limited susceptibility; they do not damage the brain and do not cause epilepsy. That is why antiseizure drugs, although they reduce recurrence, do not change the long-term outlook. The real clinical danger lies not in the seizure but in what may be causing the fever: bacterial meningitis can present with a seizure, especially in infants whose signs are subtle and in children who are not fully immunised.

guidedApproach.title: Simple versus complex, and the meningitis question
guidedApproach.guidance: A simple febrile seizure is generalised, lasts under 15 minutes and does not recur within 24 hours; about 70–75% are simple. A complex seizure is focal, lasts 15–30 minutes or recurs within 24 hours; beyond 30 minutes it is febrile status epilepticus. The examination after the seizure focuses on the fever source and on signs of central nervous system infection: neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle, a petechial rash, persistent drowsiness or a post-ictal deficit. Recurrence risk rises with age under 1 year at the first seizure, fever of less than 24 hours, a lower temperature at onset and a first-degree family history; with none of these the risk is under 15%, and with three or more it exceeds 60%.

guidedApproach.title: Less is more
guidedApproach.prompt: Which tests are needed after a febrile seizure?
guidedApproach.guidance: For most children, the only investigation needed is to find the source of fever. Lumbar puncture is standard under 6 months, should be considered at 6–12 months when Hib or pneumococcal vaccination is incomplete or unknown, and is indicated at any age with meningeal signs or when antibiotics have already been given and could mask meningitis. Blood tests (count, culture, glucose, electrolytes, calcium) and urinalysis are for when the fever source is unclear or the diagnosis uncertain. EEG has little value after a simple or first complex seizure, and neuroimaging is not routine; MRI is reserved for recurrent complex seizures with a prolonged post-ictal deficit, and CT only for suspected bleeding or a structural lesion.

guidedApproach.title: Rescue, reassurance and selective prophylaxis
guidedApproach.guidance: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is treated with a benzodiazepine: midazolam 0.2 mg/kg, IV diazepam 0.3–0.5 mg/kg or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, or rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg when there is no IV access. Most children need no regular medicine. Antipyretics such as paracetamol make the child comfortable but do not prevent recurrence, so parents should not wake a child to give them. Intermittent oral clobazam 0.3 mg/kg every 12 hours for 24 hours from the start of a fever is reserved for frequent or complex seizures or families far from care. Continuous valproate or phenobarbitone is rarely needed. The most important intervention is calm, clear counselling: what to do during a seizure, when to call for help, and that the outlook is excellent.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 20-month-old girl had a 3-minute generalised seizure with a temperature of 39.4°C and coryza. She is fully immunised, and 40 minutes later she is alert and playing with a normal examination apart from a red throat. Her father had febrile seizures. The family lives 2 km from the hospital.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate management?

options.explanation: Lumbar puncture is not needed in a fully immunised child over 12 months who has returned to normal with no meningeal signs (IAP).

options.text: EEG and MRI brain as an outpatient
options.explanation: Routine EEG and imaging have no value after a simple febrile seizure (IAP).
Continuous prophylaxis is not indicated for a simple febrile seizure (IAP).

options.text: Treat the fever source, counsel the parents and discharge with first-aid advice
options.explanation: Correct. A first simple febrile seizure over 18 months in a stable child with a reliable family does not need admission (IAP).

options.text: Paracetamol every 4 hours around the clock to prevent recurrence
options.explanation: Antipyretics do not reduce recurrence (IAP); they are for comfort only.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Manage a first simple febrile seizure without unnecessary tests or drugs.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Simple febrile seizure, normal child, reliable family: treat the cause, counsel, discharge.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 9-month-old boy has a 6-minute generalised seizure with fever of 38.8°C. He has received only his birth vaccines. After the seizure he remains irritable and drowsy for 2 hours, and the anterior fontanelle feels full. Glucose is 92 mg/dL.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Reassure and discharge after the fever settles
options.explanation: Persistent drowsiness, a full fontanelle and incomplete immunisation make meningitis likely.

options.text: Admit, perform a lumbar puncture and treat for possible meningitis
options.explanation: Correct. Under 12 months with incomplete Hib and pneumococcal vaccination and signs of meningitis, lumbar puncture is indicated (IAP).
Prophylaxis does not address the possibility of bacterial meningitis.
EEG does not diagnose meningitis and is not urgent here.

options.text: Give rectal diazepam to take home
options.explanation: The priority is diagnosis of a possible central nervous system infection.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise when a febrile seizure may be meningitis.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Under 12 months, incompletely immunised or meningeal signs: lumbar puncture.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 3-year-old boy has had three febrile seizures in the past 5 months, each generalised and lasting 2–4 minutes. Development and neurological examination are normal, there is no family history of epilepsy and there have been no afebrile seizures. The family lives 3 hours from the nearest hospital, recognise fever easily, and are very anxious about the next episode.
boardQuestions.question: Which approach is most appropriate?

options.explanation: Continuous drugs carry behavioural and cognitive side effects and are kept for failed intermittent therapy or recurrent complex seizures (IAP).
Frequent seizures (3 or more in 6 months) with poor access to care are indications for intermittent prophylaxis (IAP).

options.text: Oral clobazam 0.3 mg/kg every 12 hours for 24 hours from the start of each fever, with rescue medicine at home
options.explanation: Correct. Intermittent clobazam is used for frequent febrile seizures and poor access to care (IAP).

options.text: Paracetamol at the first sign of fever
options.explanation: Paracetamol eases discomfort, but antipyretics do not prevent recurrence (IAP).
Carbamazepine and phenytoin are not effective for febrile seizures (IAP).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Choose prophylaxis for frequent febrile seizures.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Intermittent clobazam during fevers; continuous drugs only when intermittent therapy fails.

patientEducation: During a seizure: place on side, do not put anything in the mouth, time it.
Call for help if over 5 minutes.
Fever control is for comfort, not prevention.

dischargeCriteria: Back to baseline, fever source treated, parents counselled (IAP)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review with the family paediatrician; neurology follow-up if complex features (IAP).
